..FOR EXTREME SOUTHWESTERN CALIFORNIA INCLUDING ORANGE...
SAN DIEGO...WESTERN RIVERSIDE AND SOUTHWESTERN SAN BERNARDINO
COUNTIES...

...UPDATED AVIATION, MARINE, AND BEACHES DISCUSSION...

An upper level ridge of high pressure will remain over Southern 
California into Sunday, which will continue widespread above average 
temperatures. High temperatures Saturday and Sunday will be in the 
mid to upper 70s for much of the coastal basin, with highs in the 
upper 70s to low 80s in the low desert, in the low 70s in the High 
Desert, and in the 50s and 60s across area mountains. An upper level 
low will push the ridge to our south Sunday night into Monday, which 
will kick off a period of cooler and wetter weather. 

For Monday, the overall flow will be zonal ahead of a robust closed 
low digging south across the Eastern Pacific Tuesday into Wednesday. 
Starting Monday, most inland locations will be running 3 to 7 
degrees below average and that will continue through next Saturday. 
Current forecast has the coolest day of the week on Tuesday. Chances 
of precipitation enter the forecast as early as Sunday night due to 
an influx of moisture into Southern California. A short-wave passing 
through Central California will keep atmospheric forcing minimal, 
which will keep any precipitation light. Periods of light rain are 
possible through the day Monday, but coverage is not expected to be 
widespread. First look at rainfall rates from the RRFS shows mostly 
0.15"/hr or less on Monday. NBM chances of rainfall exceeding 0.5" 
Sunday night into Monday night are 15-30%, with the higher chances 
north of San Diego County. 

Models are in fairly good agreement that an upper level closed low 
will dig south and east into Southern California Tuesday into 
Wednesday. This will bring widespread moderate to heavy rain, gusty 
winds, and mountain snow to the area. Models have shown subtle 
increases in IVT values from past runs with increasing confidence in 
seeing a weak to locally moderate atmospheric river event. The 
system is expected to move through the area, mainly from northwest 
to southeast on Tuesday, ending sometime Wednesday morning or 
afternoon. Moderate to heavy precipitation is expected during the 
low's passage, along with increased winds from the coast to the 
deserts. Additionally, increased instability and warmer ocean 
temperatures, will contribute to a greater chance for thunderstorms.
 
It continues to look likely that at least 1 inch of rain can be 
expected from the coast to the mountains. NBM chances of rainfall 
totals exceeding 3 inches Tuesday morning through Thursday morning 
are 70-80 percent across area mountains and 40 to 50 percent across 
the coast and valleys. The deserts have more spread in potential 
rainfall amounts, but have high chances of seeing at least 0.5 inch 
of rain with the low deserts having a 40-50 percent chance of 
exceeding 1 inch and the High Desert a 60-70 percent chance. 
Mountain snow is expected, with continued uncertainty in where the 
snow levels will be during the heaviest precipitation. It looks like 
snow levels will start out above 8000 ft Tuesday morning, lowering 
to around 6500 ft Tuesday night into Wednesday morning. Details on 
rain and snow will continue to be refined in the coming days. 
Continue to monitor the forecast and take time to prepare for 
potential impacts from flooding and snow for elevations 6500 ft and 
above. 

In addition to moderate to heavy rain along the coast and in the 
valleys, elevated winds can be expected Tuesday. NBM chances for 
wind gusts exceeding 35 mph Tuesday are 60-70 percent along the 
coast and 40-60 percent further inland. Elevated winds can also be 
expected over the mountains and into the deserts. The combination of 
gusty winds and saturated soils, especially in the coast and 
valleys, increases the risk of downed tree branches or shallow 
rooted trees being uprooted. 

As the storm system moves out of the area on Wednesday, a weak ridge 
may form in its place, as tropical moisture to the south lingers. 
This should bring a brief reprieve from the wet weather later on 
Wednesday into early Thursday of next week. Model ensembles continue 
to point to a troughing pattern maintaining itself across California 
for the end of next week, which may bring additional chances for 
more cooler and wetter weather.
